# PIR-2026-003: An NVLink switch tray failure took rack A15 out of service for 3 hours 16 minutes

**Status:** Approved; action items in progress · **Blameless review:** findings describe systems and procedures, not individuals. Interactive version: [Post-Incident Review page](https://jasonmossotti.github.io/dco-vendor-scorecard/pir/).

| Incident date | Ticket | Work order | MOP | Unit | Uptime severity (OSR) | Internal severity | Priority | Incident Commander | Review meeting |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-25 | INC3101173 | — | — | NVLink switch tray a15-nvsw3 | 2 Minimal | S3 (no contract breach: every response target was met) | P1 (IT Partner) | Customer Site Lead | 2026-09-29 |

*OSR 2 (Minimal): Some IT services disrupted or degraded, with minimal effect on users, customers, or reputation. One of 32 production racks was out of service; its jobs were rescheduled onto other racks. No customer-facing service, safety, or financial loss beyond the contract measurement.*

## In plain language

**What happened?** Early on September 25, one of the nine switch trays that join rack A15's 72 GPUs into a single unit failed. The rack cannot run as one machine with a switch tray missing, so the scheduler stopped sending work to all 18 of its nodes. The IT Partner replaced the tray and the rack was back in production 3 hours 16 minutes later.

**Who was affected?** The 72 GPUs in rack A15 stopped taking new work, 234.7 GPU-hours in all. Jobs were rescheduled onto other racks by the cluster's scheduler. No other rack and no customer-facing service was affected, and nobody was hurt.

**Why did it happen?** The switch tray failed in service; the replacement tray is a stocked spare and the repair itself went as it should. What the review looked at is why nothing warned us first: the rack's own health data showed no sign on this tray before it failed, and the fabric manager reports a switch tray only once it is already degraded.

**What are we doing about it?** The IT Partner is sending the failed tray back to the manufacturer and will tell us whether an early indicator exists. The Customer is checking whether the rack's health checks can watch switch trays the way they already watch GPUs, and is adding the spare count for switch trays to the weekly review so the next failure does not wait on a delivery.

## Summary (technical)

At 2026-09-25T08:10:50Z the scheduler drained all 18 nodes of rack A15 with reason 'NVLink domain degraded', 29 seconds before INC3101173 was opened as a P1 at 08:11:19Z. The IT Partner acknowledged in 4 minutes (P1 target 5) and a technician was at the rack in 4 minutes from the measured start (P1 target 15). NVLink switch tray a15-nvsw3 was replaced at 10:10:26Z (one tray out, one tray in; the failed part was tagged for return). The four return-to-service checks (leak_hold_30m, nmx_tray_health, rack_nvlink_acceptance, nccl_allreduce_rack) all passed, the last at 11:25:26Z, and the nodes were back in service at 11:26:26Z. Measured out of service is 3 h 16 min from first fault evidence, against the P1 restore target of 4 h; the ticket's own clock reports 3 h 18 min. Under FA-2 the Landlord side was healthy at T0, so the event is IT Partner-attributed. No finding was raised.

- **Trigger:** NVLink switch tray a15-nvsw3 failed in service, degrading the rack's NVLink domain.
- **Detection:** Immediate and automatic: the scheduler drained the rack 29 seconds before the ticket was opened, with the reason 'NVLink domain degraded'.
- **Resolution:** The switch tray was replaced from stock and the rack passed all four return-to-service checks before taking work again.

**Owner: IT Partner** (rules FA-2). Fault class FC-SWITCH on A15; the Landlord side was healthy at T0.

## Contract and compliance consequences


## EHS screening

- **Injuries:** 0
- **Screening:** Hot-swap of a tray in a live rack with no exposure to hazardous energy and no coolant work beyond the quick-disconnects. No injury, nothing to refer under EHS-R2.
- **Referral:** None. Screened and closed by the Customer Site Lead.

## Contributing factors

| ID | Type | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Equipment | The switch tray failed in service. The review found no alarm, no health-check failure, and no trend on this tray in the days before the failure; the failed tray was tagged for return to the manufacturer. |
| F2 | Design and identification | One switch tray out of nine takes the whole rack out of service: the 72 GPUs are one NVLink domain and cannot be split. The design is the vendor's and is not ours to change, but it means every switch tray is a rack-wide single point of failure. |
| F3 | Procedure inadequate | The rack's health checks watch GPUs and their XID codes closely, but the switch trays are reported only by the fabric manager and only once a domain is already degraded. Nothing looks at a switch tray's own counters between incidents. |

## What went well

- Detection, acknowledgement, and the technician on site all happened inside the P1 targets, and the scheduler drained the rack before anyone had to decide.
- A spare switch tray was on site, so the repair did not wait for a delivery.
- All four return-to-service checks ran and passed before the rack took work again, and the validation was attached to the ticket.

## What went poorly

- Nothing warned us: the first sign of the failure was the rack being drained.
- The spare switch tray count on site is not tracked anywhere the Customer reviews week by week.

## Where we got lucky

- The failure was on one rack's switch tray. The same failure in the leaf switches would have touched the trays of two racks.
- The rack was drained rather than killed, so running jobs finished or checkpointed instead of being lost.
